maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT

speechtext: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 62, respecting a certain trade agreement between Canada and New Zealand.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the discussion begins on the second reading of this bill, may I ask the government if they have considered a point which came up when W'e were discussing the Australian treaty. The Prime Minister at that time drew the attention of the house to the fact that where there were certain resolutions to be passed by the committee of ways and means which affected the treaty, they must be passed before the bill respecting the treaty itself would be considered. I do not mention the point to create embarrassment in any way, but where there is a rule of procedure attention ought to be drawn to it. I have before me the Prime Minister's words on the point as they are recorded in Hansard of July 15, 1931, at page 3770, as concerned the Australian treaty. My right hon. friend said:
I consulted the clerk at the table with respect to the matter, and he advised me that under the practice of this house the bill should not be proceeded with until such time as the tariff items in the agreement had been sanctioned by the committee, following which the bill to confirm the agreement will be introduced.
A little later on he said:
These resolutions are now before the committee of the house, and the proper course is to take no further step until the committee have completed consideration of the resolutions which were placed in the votes and proceedings the other evening and proceeded with yesterday by consent of the house, for which I thanked the right hon. gentleman yesterday since it enabled us to advance practically all the items.
I think there are very few items outstanding: we will dispose of those this afternoon.

To make clear that I am not seeking to embarrass the situation, in any way, I would suggest that if there is any such regulation the procedure might be regularized if the house went into committee on the resolutions and took in advance up the one or two items that are mentioned. This may not be necessary; I am not sure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I think the right hon. gentleman in this instance overlooks at least the fact that the items of wool and hides are not in the treaty at all, and therefore as far as the treaty is concerned may not be dealt with. It was because of difficulties of that character that they are in separate resolutions, which will be introduced by the Minister of Finance, and of which notice has been given as appears from the records of the house. Therefore the difficulties to which the right hon. gentleman refers do not arise.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The items, however, have been placed as they are in the resolution in consequence of something that has been done under the treaty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Yes, that is another thing. However, they are not in the treaty.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Before the Minister of Trade and Commerce proceeds with the second reading of this bill, cannot he make to the house a statement with regard to the general principles of the treaty? The desirability of a treaty with the sister dominion of New Zealand is not at all controversial. I believe the country has received with considerable satisfaction word that a treaty has been concluded, and I also believe both political parties are glad that a treaty has been consummated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Perhaps I might help the hon. gentleman. It was the intention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in moving the second reading of the bill to make a statement. Perhaps my hon. friend did not observe that he was about to do so.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Thank you.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this bill it is not my intention to go into any elaborate explanation of it. I thought the best procedure would be merely to make a very brief statement, and then when the house is in committee we shall have the material on hand to deal with any questions that may need elucidation.
The new trade agreement with New Zealand is a very simple arrangement. It includes two

New Zealand Trade Agreement
principles, which perhaps are somewhat new in trade agreements. One of them is in the Australian agreement. It is a protective clause which permits the two governments by mutual agreement to come to an understanding upon any one item that might temporarily cause embarrassment to either country. We think it is a very happy addition to trade agreements, and our experience in connection with the Australian treaty has carried out our expectations in that regard. The other principle in the New Zealand treaty, which is not included in the Australian treaty, and which we also think is of merit, is that it is possible for either country to vary the rate of duty on any item in the schedule upon giving notice to the other contracting party. Of course they are at liberty to vary the rates of duty in the tariff generally. So that the treaty is a little more elastic than any treaties that have been entered into by this country with other countries in times gone by. By this process we confidently hope that we shall avoid the necessity of abandoning what may be recognized as, generally speaking, a good agreement because of some difference over any one or more items. That is virtually all that is new or different in this agreement from any other trade agreement.
I should like to add this further observation, that the terms of this treaty have been arrived at after careful consideration by the representatives of both dominions, and we believe it represents the very best that can be secured, having in mind the interests and the rights of each country. It must be obvious of course, and no doubt is present in the minds of all hon. members, that to any bargain there must be two parties, and that neither party can expect to have everything precisely suitable to its interests and its views.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The representatives of the two dominions have endeavoured to arrive at what is thought to be fair and equitable and acceptable to both parties.
There is this also to say-and I think the house and the country should recognize it at once-that Canada being numerically and in the magnitude of its business the larger of the two dominions, naturally has perhaps a greater share in what trade will result from this interchange between the two dominions. Furthermore our products are very much more diversified, and in the manufacturing lines of course tremendously more advanced, than those of New Zealand. Consequently we shall perhaps profit more by the treaty in the volume of trade than it is possible for New 41761-157J
Zealand to do. That was recognized from the commencement. On the other hand, there are a number of articles in New Zealand of comparatively minor importance in which not much trade has developed in the past, but which we hope may develop considerably. These are items which do not conflict in any way with the products of Canada, but in relation to which up to the present very little trade has resulted. The expectation is that by settling between ourselves the status of trade benefit will accrue to both parties. I repeat also what I said the other day when the resolution was before the house, that we must not lose sight of the fact that in both instances each country accords the other the full British preference on items not recited in the schedules.
These are briefly and very sketchily the main features of the treaty. It is not with any desire to be discourteous to the house that I do not make any extended statement now; I feel it will be better to leave detailed explanations to the more informal procedure in committee of the whole, when I shall be very happy indeed to reply to any questions that may arise.
May I add this statement? Naturally we are anxious to conclude this matter as early as possible and to get the treaty into operation from Canada's standpoint for this reason above others, that this is particularly the buying season in New Zealand and in expectation of the treaty many orders are outstanding waiting the conclusion of the treaty, and it will be a distinct advantage to both countries to have it concluded at the earliest moment.
I wish therefore, Mr. Speaker, to move the second reading of the bill and to reserve to-the committee stage any detailed remarks.
Hon. CHARLES A. STEWART (West Edmonton) : Mr. Speaker, would my hon. friend mind enumerating briefly some of the more important commodities in the interchange of which we hope to obtain a larger volume of trade with New Zealand.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I should be happy to give all the details but I do submit that it would be .better to let that matter rest until we come to the schedules.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
May I point out to the minister that he has been dealing with this matter for over a year, while the members who are interested have had it before them for only twenty-four hours. It is not easy, as my hon. friend will readily understand, to appreciate difficult schedules such as these and be able to ask intelligent questions in connection with them. It does appear

New Zealand Trade Agreement
that we might be given some information now. I should not like to say what are my impressions of this treaty at the present time because they may be entirely wrong, but I think my hon. friend might indicate briefly some of the important commodities which are affected, and how they are affected as compared with the treaty which was cancelled.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I submit this is getting to a strictly committee stage and, if the hon. member would agree, I would very much prefer to deal with those questions in committee where we can talk very frankly. I hope we will go into committee very quickly; at this stage it would be difficult for me to answer the queries that may be directed by hon gentlemen opposite. I hope the house will agree to that.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
On section 1-short title.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
On this section I desire to say a few words with regard to this legislation. First I offer my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to the government as a whole for trying to improve conditions of trade in this country. That requires courage, and I am very glad they have shown that courage.
As the minister pointed out, a treaty is nothing more than a bargain; on the one side one country sells and on the other side that country buys, and the bargain must be satisfactory to both sides. Those are elementary principles with which everyone is familiar. But may I point out, quoting from memory since I have not the exact page of Hansard, that during last session I heard the Prime Minister say he had some anxiety about our trade with the Antipodes. In that respect may I say he had no one but himself to blame. What I am about to say now is nothing unpleasant; I simply desire to recall what was said during the last campaign by the right hon. gentleman and others. Yesterday I would not have made these remarks, because of an event in which we all rejoiced and which made the Prime Minister's face beam, but to-day it is different; we are about to examine cold facts. I quote from the Montreal Gazette of June 14, 1930, where I find a news item headed "Promises Repeal of Treaties Bad for Agriculture." The article is by Thomas Green, staff correspondent for the Canadian

Press, and is dated Calgary, Alberta, June 13, 1930:
In clear and emphatic terms, Hon. R. B. Bennett, Conservative leader, last night gave his pledge that if returned to power every treaty entered into by the Liberal government injurious to Canadian agriculture would be abrogated.
Canada, the Conservative leader declared, had been placed in a position of importance in respect to the tariff on agricultural products under treaties made by the Liberal administration.
"I pledge myself that every treaty entered into by the government harmful to Canadian agriculture will be abrogated if I am returned to power," he exclaimed.
Mr. Bennett scored the government for discontinuing aids to agriculture.
And so on. On July 14, 1930, according to the Montreal Gazette of July 15, the Prime Minister addressed a meeting in Sherbrooke, Quebec. One of the sub-titles of the newspaper article is "Dairymen need help." Speaking of the people who attended the meeting the article states:
They were not all Sherbrooke people. Far from it. There were many city folks, but also dairymen, from various parts of the townships, who wanted to hear some one with authority talk to them of the grievance they had so much at heart, namely New Zealand butter, for the eastern townships and Chateauguay-Huntingdon are the parts of this province which have their very existence in dairying, and many of them have been following the will-o-wisp of American trade, and when the United States put an end to this trade found themselves captured in the rear by New Zealand butter. So the dairymen were out in force.
At that meeting the right hon. Prime Minister is quoted as having said:
Do you think this government of ours has any right at all to make treaties? asked Mr. Bennett, as he proceeded to tell how the countries with which Mr. King has made treaties had raised their duties against Canadian wheat and other primary products. In all treaties the rights of Canadians had not been safeguarded, said the speaker.
The report of the meeting ends there; it is too bad it is not extended.
I wish the house clearly to understand my point. I do not blame the government for bringing in this legislation; I said that in my first remarks, and I repeat it, but during the election the stump speakers of the Conservative party were saying from every platform in the province of Quebec that if the farmers were in bad shape it was because of the New Zealand and Australian butter that was coming in, and that it was a gross mistake on the part of the government, almost amounting to treason, to let that butter enter Canada. I see my good friend from South-east Grey

New Zealand Trade Agreement
(Miss Maephail), some hon. members from Nova Scotia and others from different parts of Canada and I am sure they heard the same thing in their constituencies. I see my good friend from Compton; I am sure he made the same statements. In addition, since the opening of this parliament I have heard that view expressed by my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Thompson) who was formerly a director of the Ontario dairymen's association, by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel and by the hon. member for Chateau-guay-Huntingdon, (Mr. Moore) who all said they were against the importation of butter from the other dominions. I respect their views; I do not ask them to vote against the legislation before us to-day, but during the whole campaign the farmers were told that it was a great mistake to import so much butter from outside Canada.
Why did we import butter? Canada imported butter to a large extent-I will not quote the figures because they are well known to every hon. member-because production was not equal to consumption. It was because, when President Hoover introduced his high tariff legislation in the United States, the farmers of Maine, of New York and other states came to Canada to buy Canadian cattle. Our breeders were offered high prices for their cattle, and they sold them, and as they had less cattle the production of milk and butter consequently declined with the result that we had to import these commodities, so that the gap between production and consumption had to be filled. Tourists were coming to this country and spending, at that time, according to the statistics, two hundred million dollars, and when they asked for butter we could not expect to offer them xxle grease. That is why butter had to br .reported from the other dominions; the reason was that production had gone down in this country. That has been clearly explained. At that time, notwithstanding imports of thirty or forty million pounds, the price of blitter was twice what it is now. In 1929, the price of butter, as quoted by my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) last year, was 38-1 cents odd-I am speaking from memory. In 1930 it was 31-60, according to the figures the hon. gentleman gave last year. But when my hon. friend gave his figures of imports and exports he forgot to mention production, which, of course, is an essential point, and it was my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) who noticed this omission and brought it to the hon. gentleman's attention. A day or so after that I came in with the
statistics showing that if we had to import butter it was because, as I have just pointed out, our production was not equal to our consumption. I will not insist any more upon that; it is elementary. But during the last election every Tory speaker in every rural constituency where cattle are bred told the farmers that the Mackenzie King government has to be blamed for such importations. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) took this attitude. The Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) who is one of the ablest dairymen in Quebec, did the same. The hon. gentleman confounds water with milk-the salt water of the St. Lawrence. All these hon. gentlemen, including, I have no doubt, the hon. member from Long Lake (Mr. Cowan), said to the dairymen of the country, "You farmers are in bad shape because the Mackenzie King government is importing so much butter." An hon. member whose constituency I have forgotten, but who seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne at the first session this government was in power, also told the farmers that the King government was responsible for bringing in so much butter. I see my hon. friend from Compton (Mr. Gobeil); I am sure he said the same thing and promised to have the situation righted. He is too honest to deny it. He said to the farmers, "If you are not selling your milk and butter at a high enough price, it is because the King government is importing so much butter from Australia and New Zealand." But what did it profit the farmers here to have a Canadian market if they could not sell their butter at a reasonable price? They were not getting as reasonable a price as some people near to my hon. friend are getting for their preserves. I see my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Belec); he too, I am sure, said the same thing. Now, I do not suggest that they did not make these statements in good faith. I see my hon. friend from that fine constituency of which Prescott is the county seat (Mr. Casselman); his attitude was the same. I had occasion to speak in a certain Conservative parish, a beautiful little place, and to discuss the butter question with a distinguished lawyer from Montreal. For the first twenty minutes I spoke only about butter; I did not discuss any other subject. In his thirty minutes that gentleman was very much embarrassed to give any reply because my quotations were from Hansard; immediately after I had finished the quotations I gave him the volume so that he might make himself familiar with the situation. But

New Zealand Trade Agreement
he had nothing to say in reply. Again I ask, What does it mean to the Canadian farmer to have a market in this country if he does not receive a decent price for what he has to sell?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: What about other markets?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: My genial friend is following in the footsteps of the Prime Minister; when he is asked a question which he cannot answer he asks one himself.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I am not ashamed.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: He admits it.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I do not wish to be disagreeable to the hon. gentleman, but he knows that on every platform members of his party were saying to the farmers that the reason they were not getting a decent price for their butter was that the Mackenzie King government was importing so much of this commodity from Australia and New Zealand; it was because of the competition. Was not that what was said?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: At the time, yes.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman for his admission; he is a very good witness. But he is more candid than he was when that statement was being made. At that time he was either dishonest or ignorant, and I do not know whether it is a greater insult to be called ignorant or otherwise.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Coming from you, it does not matter.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Nescient, perhaps. I met these people on every platform, and this is what they were saying: "Shame to those in power! Let us put a stop to this." I see an hon. gentleman from one of the constituencies in British Columbia. He is interested in this matter and I am sure that he will tell us that in that province the catchword given by the then leader of the Conservative party, the present Prime Minister, was, "We will abrogate these treaties as soon as we come into power." But there was no necessity to abrogate them because Mr. Dunning, the Minister of Finance of that day, had declared on May 1, 1930, in the course of his budget speech, that he had given notice to the governments of New Zealand and Australia that the agreements would come to an end after six months' notice. But what was most important was this, that we had then a very good trade with Australia and New Zealand; those dominions were purchasing many commodities from us, such as pulpwood, paper and so forth. The reason Mr. Dunning did not cancel the treaties completely but inti-

mated instead that they would be concluded in six months was that he wished to have some satisfactory agreement evolved in the meantime at the Imperial conference of 1930, so far as these two dominions were concerned. It was most essential that we should retain our trade with these dominions, and what I sincerely regret is that at the time the present government came into power a serious mistake was made through the absence from his department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That minister was ill, and I do not know which one of his colleagues took charge of his department, but a mistake was made by someone who knew nothing about trade. I am sure that if the Minister of Trade and Commerce had been in Ottawa, thing* would have been very different, and this country would have kept its trade with New Zealand and Australia, so that it would not have been necessary to introduce this legislation this year. These arrangements should have been made last year according to an agreement previously entered into at the time of the Imperial conference. However, we must take things as they are. I congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce upon being persuasive enough to make the Prime Minister understand that trade with other countries is essential and that the Canada first policy, the erection of high tariff walls around this country, is a mistake which should be remedied.
I come again to what was said on the Tory stumps during the'last campaign. It was stated l'agriculture se meurt dans la province de Quebec-agriculture is dying in the province of Quebec. This was the statement made by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil), the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Belec), and by other hon. members from the rural constituencies and I have no doubt the hon. member for Long Lake said the same thing.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I never heard of it.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend
would not be saying that in French, but I have no doubt he said it in English. He would not complain that agriculture was dying in the province of Quebec, he would rejoice in it. Probably he issued circulars to the effect that agriculture was dying in the province of Saskatchewan. There is one minister of the crown, the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) who understands the French language, and I am sure he is fully aware of what was distributed during the last campaign by the central Conservative office. I heard so much during the last campaign that I cannot help

New Zealand Trade Agreement
but quote from the publications issued by the Tory party in Quebec. One of these reads as follows:
(Translation)
Australian Treaty-Dairy Industry
The Canadian market has been handed over to the Australian farmers; we are permitted to sell our printing machinery, automobile parts and paper on the Australian market. It is a bargain of dupes.
Canada is an agricultural country and we should keep our domestic markets for the benefit of our farmers.
In order to obtain advantages abroad for three Canadian industries, we sacrificed to Australia our dairy industry and home markets, and this, to the detriment of our farmers who make up 63 per cent of our population.
This Australian treaty, at its face constitutes an economic error; at least the King government could put up the plea that Australia had conceded to us certain advan-
To-day, owing to the shortsighted policy of the Dominion government, our dairy industry has been ruined through intensive competition by New Zealand; the millions of dollars paid out to protect our farmers serve in transporting to our markets, in cold storage, thanks to Canadian grants, butter and other foreign dairy products.
The disbursements made by our people are utilized to develop foreign dairy industries, to our detriment.
How can we explain such a faulty system;
This is the reason for the order in council benefiting New Zealand, and the treaty favouring Australia.
I try to follow the teachings of the Lord by loving my neighbour as myself but I find that although I may love Tories, I cannot love Toryism. Most of the Tories I know are very likeable, but Toryism is very hateful. I quote again:
(Translation)
Canadian modern liberalism has set in motion a system of administration disastrous in its effects, which, however, affords to the leaders of the system an opportunity of praising up the government by displaying the seemingly genuine results of an artificial prosperity. Our natural resources were exploited without discretion or discernment, to the advantage of foreigners and to the detriment of our people. Our forests have been cut without making any provision for reforestation; our Liberal governments granted vast timber concessions; the keen competition of timber limit owners, created an overproduction of paper, and the market being unable to absorb the entire output, manufacturers had to lower their prices. This decrease in prices made the payment of interest on bonds issued, uncertain, resulting in the discontinuance of dividends on preferred and common stocks. Finally we had to solve what is known as "the paper crisis."
Federal Liberalism to avert the disaster which threatened provincial Liberalism, had to find markets for the overproduction of _ our paper and thus preserve the profitable friendship of timber limit owners.
The Liberal party was doing its best to improve trade in connection with paper, pulpwood and so on, but because of this action it was strongly attacked. The article continues; (Translation)
There lies the reason of the Australian treaty, it explains the order in council granting to New Zealand, without receiving anything in return, the same advantages that we had conceded to Australia in schedule II of the treaty.
Liberalism boasts of being the _ true and disinterested protector of all that is dear to us, yet it sacrificed lightly the vast natural resources that Providence had placed at our disposal. Liberalism boasts of taking a great interest in the farming class of our province, yet it sacrificed the dairy industry of Quebec to the benefit of the New Zealand farmers. Liberalism loudly proclaims its ostentatious patriotism; it also gave evidence of being very fond of the people at election time, only _ to obtain their support and vote. Liberalism exhausts its lungs in proclaiming its disregard of private interest, yet it leaves the masses in the lurch so as to set aside for its own advantage -the farsighted and generous friendship ol the privileged few whom it has gorged with favours of all kinds, in order to enable it, when the opportunity arrives, to draw from them election contributions of which it is so fond. The country is bled to death, Liberalism is maintained in power.
As I see a good Liberal with the hon. Postmaster General, I Shall inquire from each of them, whether it is not a fact that, in their respective counties, the Conservative party distributed this campaign literature? They are unable to deny the fact.
The following is another extract of this document:
(Translation)
Agriculture is dying: who killed it?
Farmers: read what follows, and you will know how and by whom this crime was committed!
Ever since 1925, the King government has forced on parliament the Australian treaty and adopted by order in council the New Zealand convention.
By these treaties, the King government handed over the Canadian market to foreigners, in exchange for a few miserable concessions to industry.
What I have quoted will give an idea of the literature which was distributed throughout every rural parish, municipality or borough in the province of Quebec, and I have no doubt the same publications in English were distributed to the English farming districts. One thing that strikes me in connection with this butter question is the fact that the Tory party used this commodity as a stepping stone to power. During the campaign it was said that the Canadian markets were of no interest, the results were what counted. The fact is that the farmer received much more for his butter when we were importing sufficient to make up the difference between production and consumption than he does now when the production equals or perhaps is more than the consumption. The hon. member for Compton said during the

New Zealand Trade Agreement
campaign that we must have Canadian markets. At the same time he used despicable words about lawyers. I am a lawyer, I defend farmers and if the hon. member is still a farmer, I shall attempt to defend him against himself. It is hard work for a lawyer to delve into these statistics in order to get at the truth, but I do this with pleasure in order to show my electors, who are farmers, the deep interest I take in their welfare.
The other day I asked the Minister of Marine why he was saying that the government had stopped the importation of butter. They did not stop it completely; some butter still comes in. Otherwise the new treaties could be considered as a joke by Australia and New Zealand. An hon. member points out it is somewhat strange that although we are on an export basis, we still import some butter. The plain question I asked the Minister of Marine, was this: "Are you in favour of a reasonable price for butter with importations, or a very low price without importations?" The answer he gave me was this: "I am in favour of a reasonable price and I am against importations." Fancy a minister of the crown saying that, when he knows very well that last year the house had voted for a treaty with Australia and that it was ready to vote for one to-day with New Zealand! I do not wish my words to be misconstrued; I am not against this treaty; I know we must make some sacrifices in the matter of trade, because trade cannot be one-sided. I know the minister is well disposed, but I speak about those who deceived the people during the last election by making false statements regarding the dairy business. A moment ago I mentioned that Mr. Dunning, in his budget speech of May 1, 1930, said that he had notified Australia and New Zealand that the treaty would come to an end six months after the notice was given, and in the meantime the duty on butter was increased. The duty was four, six and seven cents a pound, and when the present government came into power, they increased that duty to eight, twelve and fourteen cents a pound. The duty under the Dunning budget did not please the people because it was not enough. The Tories were saying on every hustings: The duty is not enough; we will increase it in order that you may receive a fair price for butter. The ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce, I am sure, has heard the same statement made. Every one on this side who has been on the same platform with a Conservative speaker at a joint meeting, has heard him say the same thing. They were deceiving the people; they were saying that as soon
as the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister, gets into power, he will raise the duty on butter in order that the farmers may receive not less than forty of forty-five cents, and perhaps fifty or sixty cents a pound for their butter. In my constituency, a Tory candidate said: I shall see to it that the leader of the Conservative party raises the duty in order that you may get at the very least forty cents a pound for your butter. What does it mean to a farmer if he does not get a decent price for it? What does it mean to the hon. member for Compton? His friends will laugh at him. They will say:	The
Canadian market as it is means nothing to you because you get nothing out of it.
The Tory government were true to their word; they increased the tariff; the four cents became eight cents, the six cents became twelve and the seven became fourteen, or twice as much. Then what happened? This is mentioned in a return that I received last year and that was signed by the Secretary of State, showing that when the tariff on butter was the highest, the price was the lowest. It is perhaps on account of that return that the Prime Minister should be advised by his supporters that they have decided to return to the Liberal policy of reducing tariffs in order to secure trade. Last year the duty on butter under the Australian treaty was five cents, notwithstanding the fact that the Australian government is paying a premium on this commodity; this year under the New Zealand treaty the duty is also five cents.
I do not wish to detain the committee much longer on this, but to sum up, let me say that the Canadian people were grossly deceived by every Conservative speaker in Quebec and in each of the eight sister provinces, when they said first of all, that it was due to imports of butter that the price was low, and when they told the people that under a high tariff the price of butter would be reasonable, just as good as it was the previous year. The people were deceived both ways and now this legislation is introduced into the house. I have no objection to it; it is an experiment and we shall see how it works, but I regret the, if I may say so, silly satements that were made first by the Prime Minister and repeated by his own organization under the control of General McRae in order to deceive the people. This is the feature I oppose most strongly. The public can now see that the guiding star of liberalism is still leading the Conservative party when they want to do the proper thing; to do this they have to come back to the old Liberal trade policy. fMr. I. A. Mackenzie.]
The difficulty in negotiating a treaty of this kind with New Zealand is pre-eminently due to the fact that New Zealand, more than any other country of which I know, is wholly agricultural and pastoral in its exports, so anything it exports to Canada must come directly in conflict with agriculture hi this country, which makes it very difficult to deal with the situation. I would have been interested if the minister had replied when the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) asked him to amplify, or even illustrate, what lines of business from New Zealand he expected would be increased in consequence of this treaty, because I know, from some examination and after having lived there, how little New Zealand can export that will not come in direct competition with one branch or another of agriculture in Canada.
I think the only three products that New Zealand exports and which we do not produce ourselves are rabbits, flax and kauri gum, which is a minor product used in making scents and soaps. It is dug up in the swamps of New Zealand, so we need not grudge them that trade. The same applies to rabbits, so long as they are not brought here alive. With regard to the flax, I am sorry to see anything done to facilitate its entry to this country. It is an inferior article, and has one almost dangerous quality about it. It will make apparently strong rope, which will stand a heavy strain if that strain is applied gradually, but it has the unusual quality of snapping like a lead pencil if you give it a sudden jerk. It is a native product, grown in the swamps of that country.
I would like to make only one comment in regard to the preliminary part of the treaty, and then there are one or two comments which I have to make when we come to the particular items, which I hope we will be permitted to take up one by one. I notice that we are given a preference on Canadian lumber, but unless I am wrong that preference is arrived at by leaving the duty against Canadian lumber where it was and increasing the duty against lumber from other countries. Of course that does give some preference, but it is not one highly calculated to increase the demand for our product.
Then there is the question of our fish. Probably there is a plausible explanation, but after examining the item here I do not understand it. The minister comes from British Columbia, and he must be sufficiently familiar with the need for a preference on British Columbia salmon to see that this preference is given, but the item rather puzzles me. By this item

New Zealand Trade Agreement
New Zealand gives us a preference on "fish, potted and preserved, namely salmon, including any liquor, oil or sauce." Our canned salmon is n-ot potted or preserved; there is as much difference between preserved fish and canned salmon as there is between jam and canned fruit. It seems to me that canned salmon should come-under item 35a, which deals with "canned fish, not including fish paste," but as I say I am sure there must be some explanation, and I only mention the matter so it will not be lost sight of.
I also notice that the preference on this preserved salmon is very small; it is not nearly as large as the preference given by Australia. I see that under item 123 we give New Zealand a preference on shell fish known as toheroas, in sealed tin containers. We let that article in free, but they do not let our main fish product in under the same terms. The articles in which British Columbia is particularly interested are lumber, fish, paper and pulp. Pulp enters New Zealand free in any case, so we get no preference there, and no preference is given to newsprint. There are six paper items, and we are given a preference on only one. These are the things that somewhat detract from what we bad hoped we would get from this treaty.
There is one other comment I should like to make with regard to articles IV and VII. Article IV deals with the method by which the government proposes to stop the importation of goods when such goods are coming in to the injury of our citizens. Under the Australian treaty that section stated that goods, the produce or manufacture of Australia, imported under the provisions of article I, should not be subject to the provisions of section 6 of the customs tariff of Canada. That section excluded the application of the dumping duty. In the New Zealand treaty the wording is different:
. . . shall not be subject to section 6 of the customs tariff of Canada unless previous notice has been given by the government of Canada to the government of New Zealand that the importation of such goods would prejudicially or injuriously affect the producers or manufacturers of similar goods in Canada, and if, at the expiration of a period of thirty days from the elate of such notice, remedial measures satisfactory to the government of Canada are not put into effect . . .
Then Canada can apply the dumping duty.

They give New Zealand thirty days notice, and if at the end of that time remedial measures have not been taken the dumping duty goes into effect. That would seem to give a man whose goods were on the water at least thirty dlays in which to have those goods received and sold in Canada, but there is a further clause included:
At the option of the government of Canada any importation thus complained of, other than perishable goods, may be held in bond during the said period of thirty days.
That is the objectionable feature. It will be possible for this government, without notice at all, to increase the duty over night on an article already on the water, by the application of the dumping duty.
The British government-it has been alluded to here-has already expressed the opinion, or perhaps the hope, in connection with the coming conference, that Canada will abandon the system of enforcing the dumping duty overnight, so to speak, because it leads to great uncertainty when a man buys goods and does not know, while they are on the water in transit, what is likely to be done by means of that duty. It has always been held that a somewhat unreasonable tariff is preferable to a state of uncertainty, when it is not known whether the tariff may go up or down suddenly. Under the Australian treaty they had to give three months' notice and not thirty days; and under that treaty they could not hold goods in bond. But now, to-morrow morning, it could suddenly be announced, "We will give you thirty days' notice and hold your goods in bond, unless they are perishable, and at the end of that time we will apply the dumping duty." primage, or is it extra?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Primage is applicable to
free goods while the surtax is applicable to dutiable goods. In connection with item 333 (1) cultivators, harrows, ploughs, drills, sowers, seed or green cleaners and separators, it will be seen that the rate to the United States is 42-87 per cent while the rate to Canada is 36-75 per cent. We would have liked to have had a better rate but that was the best we could get. We are given an advantage against the United States, which is our main competitor in this class of goods. The next item is one in which we are interested. It reads:
Unspecified agricultural implements, including ploughs, cultivators and seed drills, handworked; ploughs, single furrow mouldboard, not exceeding 266 pounds; also certain parts of ploughs or harrows.
This item is free with a 3 per cent primage.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
It is the same all the
way through?

speechtext:
It is free as against the
other item which is dutiable.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Ploughs and cultivators appear in both items; how can they be subject to two separate duties?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is a different classification. Automobiles is perhaps the most important item to us and I am at liberty to state that the rates are satisfactory to the Canadian producer. A large proportion of the automobiles which we will export to New Zealand will come under the 75 per cent Canadian content class which it will be noted carries a rate of 20 per cent in the case of Canada and 40 per cent in the case of the United States. In the case of the 50 to 75 per cent Canadian content, we have an advantage as against the United States but some disadvantage as against Great Britain. However, the cars manufactured in Canada are not the type manufactured in Great Britain and our main competitor is the United States.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That rate
is not any lower than what we enjoyed formerly.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I will have that information looked up and give my hon. friend an answer later on. The hon. member for

New Zealand Trade Agreement
Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has referred to the fact that it is difficult to find items which New Zealand could export and which would not be competitive with Canadian goods. There is no doubt that was one of the difficulties with which we were confronted, but we believe we have worked it out as satisfactorily as possible.
I was rather sorry to hear the hon. member's comments in connection with New Zealand hemp. I have taken some trouble to investigate this matter and I find that New Zealand hemp has proven satisfactory to a number of large manufacturers. During the past year I went out of my way to get our manufacturers to interest themselves in the importation of New Zealand hemp. Although this hemp may not be as good as the sisal from Mexico and the hemp from Manilla in [DOT]the manufacturing of binder twine, as it has a tendency to curl when it is passing through the eyes of the binder-

Mr. BROWN. Why is binder twine allowed to come in free under all schedules?

At the request of New

twine from New Zealand?

speechtext: I will have that information looked up.

speechtext:
No, not necessarily. I
think hon. members should keep in mind the fact that we hope to develop considerable business in lines which have not previously been developed. I do not wish to harp on this point, but I must say that we have been importing a large variety of goods from the United States and it was felt that a large part of this business might profitably go to New Zealand.
I can assure the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that the lumber item is entirely satisfactory to the British Columbia interests, and

I think to the eastern interests as well although they are not affected in the same way. The same observation applies to fish. The description in schedule B is the precise description used in the tariff nomenclature of New Zeal-land, and there is no question but that it includes canned salmon.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The minister will admit that it uses the words "potted and preserved"?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That is quite true, but
it includes salmon.

speechtext:
It says preserved or potted

speechtext:
In New Zealand potted
and preserved is the description used for canned.

speechtext:
There is an item of
canned salmon in the New Zealand customs schedule; what does that refer to?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I am speaking from
memory, but I do not think canned salmon is mentioned.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speechtext: Item 35 (a) covers fish, canned, not including fish paste.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That is unique to the
trade agreement between New Zealand and Australia and does not enter into the general schedule; it is left out entirely.
Paper is provided for in the treaty under a satisfactory arrangement. I would remind the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that while a very wide range of paper is not mentioned in the schedule, we get the British preference in regard to the whole of that classification, and this will be of distinct advantage to Canada.
Reference was made to article IV and my hon. friend was under some apprehension that the operation of this would not be satisfactory. I believe he indicated he thought perhaps it was a little unfair. Let me give a brief explanation in regard to it. Article IV must be compared with the article in the Australian treaty dealing with the suspension of section 6 of the customs tariff, that is the dumping clause. It will be noted that in the Australian treaty section 6 is completely suspended and abandoned as far as Australia is concerned, but that article IX, which makes provision for notice where a commodity is being imported prejudicially to the interests of the importing country, provides a remedy in that the commodity goes under the general tariff. In the New Zealand treaty the matter

New Zealand Trade Agreement
is dealt with somewhat differently. Section 6 is suspended, but only after notice and then, at the expiration of the notice, which is only one month as against three months in the Australian treaty, all the dumping clause provisions of the Canadian tariff apply. This is a different method of treatment, but it is the formula presented to us by New Zealand when we were negotiating and the principle being more or less the same, we accepted the New Zealand formula which I think is, shall I say, a little more rigid than that in the Australian treaty. It is different, but equally effective.

speechtext:

course my hon. friend will bear this in mind: it is the injured country, so to speak, that will give the notice. If they give the notice in writing, that is their funeral, if I may use that expression. If they are anxious to give the notice, they will cable and the period of thirty days is an added protection to the importing country; inasmuch as it has been accepted there can be no complaint on the part of the other country.

speechtext:
I have no objection to the
minister using the dumping clause instead of the other method that he used in the Australian treaty, but I should like him to answer this question:	Will the method adopted of
having only thirty days' notice and having the stuff in bond, not have the effect that the dumping provision can be imposed at a moment's notice and that this will lead to disintegration and uncertainty of trade? That is the point.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I think not. The theory
behind that is this, that the exporting country, whether Canada in the one case or New Zealand in the other, may be presumed to 41761-158
export certain goods on consignment. If they export on consignment, there should be no objection to those goods immediately on arrival being placed in bond until such time as the holder, the consignee, is prepared to enter them for consumption. Otherwise this might happen-

speechtext: He might lose his sale?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
No, the goods might be
exported on consignment and be allowed to lie indefinitely in the importing country, with the latter being able to take no action, but the presence of a large quantity of consigned goods in any market always has an injurious effect upon prices in the importing country where those goods are, as it were, hanging over the market. It was to obviate the danger of that that this form was adopted.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
But in case of selling goods
on order, would not a hardship be created if the duty were raised while the goods were in transit?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: We must read the article in this sense: first, it must be shown that the importation of the goods is going to affect injuriously manufacturers or producers in the importing country. That is the basis of the whole thing. Then a thirty-days' notice is given by cable-it is presumed in every case it would be given immediately by cable- that such goods are entering prejudicially. Then it is expected that the two countries by agreement will apply some remedial action. That is, we will assume these goods are billed at a figure that is calculated to injure the importing country. The exporter might undertake not to release the goods except at a price that was consistent with or similar to that of goods in the importing country.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The minister must remember that those goods may be already sold by the importer. What will he do to fulfil his contract?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Any importer of goods-

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Three months.

speechtext:
But I am speaking of
importing in the absence of a treaty. The importing country might change the tariff

while the goods were in transit whether they were sold or not, so that in this nothing is being imposed upon the importer that is not present against him whether the treaty were in force or not.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I submit to the minister that the very idea of a treaty is to give assurance of sale and certainty of business at a known rate of duty, so that business can be conducted and contracts entered into and carried out. If under the treaty anything is permissible that may destroy the business Canada enjoys with New Zealand, it is dangerous. The government of New Zealand might destroy a Canadian contract.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That feature is present,
but I would point out to my hon. friend that it is equally present whether you have a treaty or not.

speechtext:
Under the treaty you have
three months.

speechtext: In the absence of a treaty that same eventuality might occur, so there is not imposed by this any risk on an exporter that is not present in normal trade. The provisions of the treaty, of course, postulate cordiality, good will and common sense, and a friendly attempt to adjust any difficulties. That is the basis of the whole thing. It provides for a friendly method of adjusting what might otherwise be a provocative and difficult situation.

My hon. friend will find

By increasing the valuation you increase the regular duty, and then add the dumping duty. This particular section says that you will not add the dumping duty, but it does not say that the other sections shall not apply.

where the duty is ad valorem, and in such cases the minister will have power to shut the goods out at will.

speechtext:
I would like the minister
to complete his speech by telling us something about butter. In the last election in the province of Quebec twenty candidates of the Conservative party won their seats in this house on this question of New Zealand butter, and I would ask the minister to tell me how the position is going to be changed by this treaty. Will the farmer be completely saved by this change in duty on butter, from one to five cents, or what is going to happen?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The answer to that very
reasonable question is that under the old treaty the duty on butter was one cent a pound and under this treaty it is five cents a pound. That is the first point. Then under the provisions of article IV there are remedial rates which may be exercised. Furthermore, as was quoted a short while ago by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, the dairy council -when they appeared before the tariff board represented that a four cent rate was sufficient. Presumably, therefore, a five cent rate should be reasonable protection, and in the case of emergency we have remedial powers under article IV.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Do I understand, then, that this treaty practically means the prohibition of the importation of New Zealand butter into Canada, that there will be no importations from New Zealand under this new rate? Conditions have entirely changed from what they were when we were importing New Zealand butter into Canada. Then the

New Zealand Trade Agreement
farmers in the eastern townships were exporting their cream to the United States because they could get a better price and we had no Canadian butter in this country, so we imported butter from New Zealand; but now butter is being exported from Canada. We have enough Canadian butter for ouselves, and if this new rate means that importations of butter from New' Zealand will be shut out, I do not see what advantage the treaty will be to the dairy farmer.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Might I answer the hon. member who a moment ago asked for the rates on motor cars

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The minister is slipping.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I do not understand that my hon. friend from Bona venture expects an answer, but if he does I find myself in a very happy position. He asks what our expectations are. We anticipate that under this treaty the rather troublesome difficulties of the last two years will vanish, that the relations between Canada and New Zealand will be amicable in all respects, and that the interests of all parties will be adequately safeguarded and protected. Reasonable provision is made for adjusting any difficulties which may arise. In regard to the duty on motor cars, the duty was formerly 50 per cent on all cars. The new rate under the schedule is 26 per cent when there is 75 per cent or over of Canadian content, and 32 per cent when the Canadian content is from 50 to 75 per cent.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I see that onions are mentioned in the treaty. Has the hon. member for South Essex been consulted about that?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: That is a very important item. We get a special rate on onions entering New Zealand, and New Zealand gets a preference on their onions coming here, but we do a much larger business with New Zealand in onions than they do with us. It is one of those cases where there is a reciprocal trade which is advantageous to both countries.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It pleases me.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Potatoes are not mentioned in the treaty. The farmer is now getting only a few cents per bushel for his potatoes. Was any attempt made to develop a market in New Zealand for Canadian potatoes?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: We get the British preferential rate.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Does that mean we are going to export any potatoes to New Zealand?
41761-158J

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: If our exporters are enterprising enough and the market in New Zealand is attractive enough, there is a possibility, but frankly I would not expect a very much enlarged market for our potatoes in the Antipodes. There is a duty on potatoes entering New Zealand.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Is there any news regarding the potato situation? The situation in Quebec and New Brunswick is critical. New Brunswick No. 1 potatoes are retailing in Ottawa at 50 cents per 80 pounds. I wonder what the New Brunswick farmer is getting out of that. Is there any prospect of getting a market in Cuba or anywhere else for our potatoes?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I should not like to digress too far into a discussion of matters outside of the treaty, but I will answer my hon. friend by saying we are doing everything that is possible at the moment in that regard. There is a special effort being made in regard to Cuba, but I am afraid that the season is too far gone for us to expect to do much business in potatoes with Cuba this year. There is no question that the potato situation is bad, but we are doing everything we can. We have succeeded in assisting in the marketing of some of the potato crop in the maritimes, not of course to the degree that we should have liked, but we have done everything that was possible. I would rather deprecate, Mr. Chairman, getting into a discussion of items outside of the treaty.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I see potatoes are not mentioned in the treaty at all.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is the British preferential rate for potatoes.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Is there any news from England about the potato situation?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: We are working on that. It is a very difficult task.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I am glad to notice in this treaty that the government is now recognizing the value of trade, even if it is concerned with the same articles, because in tariff discussions that have taken place in the house during the last ten years it has been frequently objected by hon. members on the other side that goods were coming into Canada in certain quantities, although similar or even greater quantities of the same class of goods were going out of Canada. I think this marks an advance in the trade thinking of hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Thank you very much. All compliments are welcome.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I am quite well aware that the high duty on eggs from the United States will prevent any importations from that country, but in previous years we have received large importations during the winter months, December, January and February. I well remember that when I was soliciting a certain gentleman's vote during the last election he told me he would not vote for any government that let so many eggs in, and so I lost his support. I want to make sure that the government is not going to imperil its existence by allowing too many eggs to come in from New Zealand under this arrangement during those months when our poultrymen get their best prices and depend upon these returns to carry them through. I think in this morning's Journal I noticed the secretary of the National Dairy Council expressed some regret that the protection against condensed and powdered milk and casein had not been made higher.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is made lower.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT

speechtext: I am in the very happy position of being able to assure my hon. friend by indubitable evidence that there is not any need for apprehension about eggs. The facts regarding eggs are as I have already stated them. Eggs from New Zealand have been free for many years.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The duty was very low from the United States.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: In the fiscal year 1930 Canada imported eggs to the value of $950,000, of which 98 per cent came from the United States and none from New Zealand.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Under what rate from the United States?

NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It was hardly worth bothering with then.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Quite true. With regard to powdered milk, we have no representations objecting in any way to the item referred to.

speechtext: I was mentioning what I read in the paper this morning.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister, I think, fully appreciates the fact that my sympathies are very much with him in his work of negotiating a treaty with the sister dominion of New Zealand. I was disappointed that he had not made just as full a statement at the outset as he has made now with regard to the features of the treaty which distinguish It from the old treaty, and which he expects will be helpful to Canada in enabling this country to secure a greater share of trade from New Zealand and on the other hand will be helpful to New Zealand in enabling that country to secure a large share of our trade.
I propose to make a few general observations with regard to the treaty itself and its desirability, which is not questioned by any hon. member in the house, nor indeed, I think by the Canadian people. I shall not worry my hon. friend the minister in putting through his treaty, with the same kind of political criticisms that we had to face from several hon. gentlemen on the other side, especially the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), when the previous treaty was under discussion. We were told that the government then in power was destroying Canadian agriculture and the butter industry because we imported some of our butter from New Zealand. The minister is not going to be worried by me with any unfair criticism at all. I quite realize what the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said, that the sister dominion of New Zealand is a country of whose total exports 92 per cent are pastoral products. There are such exports as kauri gum and hemp, but these are infinitesimal compared with the pastoral products which New Zealand exports. New Zealand raises sheep and is probably one of the finest sheepraising countries in the world. Therefore she exports wool and mutton. New Zealand raises cattle; therefore she must sell hides and beef. New Zealand has probably the finest dairy herds that can be found out of doors, and therefore all dairy products, whether cheese, butter, condensed milk and milk products must be a substantial part of her export trade. No hon. gentleman on the opposite side or on this side can expect any minister of trade and commerce, past, present or future, to make a deal with the sister dominion of New Zealand without holding out some hope to that dominion that we will endeavour to take a substantial amount of these products, and no politician need go among the farmers of this dominion and tell them that their com-

New Zealand Trade Agreement
modities will not have to compete with commodities imported from New Zealand if a satisfactory trade treaty is arranged. Therefore I am glad to have the minister stand up in the house and be as frank and as honest about the question as he was in his opening remarks when he said that any trade treaty must be a case of give and take.
But there is a feature which is helpful in promoting trade between this country and New Zealand-namely that our respective seasons are opposite to each other. This feature does relieve the situation to some extent. We can export apples to New Zealand at the very time they are required; and New Zealand can export apples to us at the very time when our apples are not ripening. There are only two or three months in the year when we have not a surplus of eggs and at that time New Zealand's hens are laying. Hansard contains a speech made by me when I was in my hon. friend's position refuting the accusation that we were allowing tremendous importations of eggs. Canada never imported many eggs. Canada always started to accumulate eggs for storage in April, and by December had 175,000,000 to 200,000,000 dozen in storage. True, in January and February we may have run short, and then we probably imported a million dozen or so from the United States. I say to my hon. friend the minister that if the eggs that formerly came from the United States can now be imported from New Zealand, I shall be very glad he has made the arrangement. Likewise in connection with any other commodities which we have to import, I would rather import them from a sister dominion than from a foreign country, whether it be New Zealand apples rather than Oregon apples, or New Zealand eggs rather than American.
There is another point with respect to the treaty that has been referred to in this discussion, which the minister has to a considerable extent cleared up; that is stability of trade is very desirable at the present time. Someone said recently-which I think must appeal to every man who is facing the difficulties of government or of business at the present time-that prosperity was largely based on faith plus activity, and that depressions were usually caused by fear plus inactivity. If business is to progress by satisfactory trade arrangements with New Zealand or with the other parts of the British Empire w'ho will be represented at the conference to be held here this summer, there must be some faith in the country, and there must be some faith in governmental legislation which will allow trade to flow with the fewest possible obstacles. In making a treaty with New
Zealand I think the minister would do well to remove from the treaty every particle of influence of order in council legislation, and let the people of New Zealand and the people of Canada know exactly what will be the rates of duty, for the period of a year. It is all very well to talk about emergencies. Emergencies may arise, but when an Australian exporter comes to Canada and establishes a market, whether it be for eggs, for butter or for condensed milk, he comes here with the understanding that his government has made an arrangement with the Canadian government whereby he may do business. If, after he has begun to distribute his product throughout Canada, some producer of that product in Canada makes a strong appeal to the minister the whole question is held up for negotiation. I submit to my hon. friend that this is not very encouraging to the man who has come here to sell his goods. On the other hand if a Canadian exporter establishes agencies in New Zealand and arranges contracts, and then someone in Australia suddenly discovers that the import comes into competition with industries already established, to have the whole question reopened is not very satisfactory to the Canadian exporter. Therefore may I submit to the minister that my principal criticism of his treaty is that the rates of duty are not definitely established. The privilege contained in sections 35 to 40 referred to of putting a value on goods by order in council in my opinion may destroy the advantages offered in the treaty. We should know definitely that we are going to have an established rate of duty into Canada, and that when New Zealand starts to do business it will not be injured by the application of the dumping duty or by an increased valuation being placed on imports.
W'hat business may be done in Canada in condensed milk I do not know, but I do not think the business in ibutter will bother anyone, because the fallacy of everything that was said from the other side of the house during 1929 and 1930 has been amply demonstrated, and I have no desire to rub it in. At that time we had general prosperity in Canada. I defended the old New Zealand treaty which was an extension of the Australian treaty, and I will defend my hon. friend's treaty when he works out the details. We must buy something from our sister dominion. Under the old treaty Canada was enjoying prosperity greater than was enjoyed by any other country with a similar population. We were consuming thirty-five or thirty-six pounds of butter per capita in this country, and we were not producing enough
New Zealand Trade Agreement

butter to meet the demand. No country in the world ever had such a high per capita consumption of butter. The reason we were importing butter was very simple. There had grown up a trenmendous consumption of fresh milk. The condensed milk business was built up and was taking a large part of the flow of milk of many of the best herds in some of the best dairy districts in Canada. As the hon. .member for Gaspe said, there was a large volume of cream going from the eastern townships to the United States, and the use of ice cream was rapidly increasing. All these lines of business were more profitable to the Canadian milk producer than was the production of butter, even at the price then obtaining. As a result Canada was short of butter to the extent of some thirty to fifty million pounds yearly. Butter importations amounted to about one-sixth of our consumption, and as a result of that importation we were doing a good business with New Zealand in manufactured goods. I said in the house and on the hustings, and I say now to my hon. friend the minister, that if he does have to import dairy products and as a result of this import he can increase the volume of manufactured goods, being sold to a sister dominion, the workmen who will manufacture these goods in Canada will consume much of the condensed milk and butter and eggs imported, so on the whole the trade will be a good trade.
I hope that never again in this country or in this house will we have the exhibition of hypocrisy and insincerity that we had in connection with the criticism of our importation of butter from New Zealand. I shall not offer my hon. frend the minister any political criticism with regard to his treaty, such as was offered to us; when he is prepared to take his treaty item by item and explain the reasons which actuated him in arriving at his decisions, I think he will find that we will agree that in most instances he has made a splendid treaty. Why should we object? This government is continuing the policy which we inaugurated. I know very well that many items are included in the present treaty which were not included in the Australian treaty.
Undoubtedly it was desirable to have a new treaty with New Zealand. Agriculture is predominant in that country; it is not quite so much so in Australia, and it is not so prominent in Canada. In other words, Canada has a larger percentage of manufactured products than either of our sister dominions, Australia is following closely in our wake,

but New Zealand is not so close. Therefore the treaty which might be made by the minister with Australia might not suit the requirements of trade with New Zealand. In 1925 Canada extended the terms of the Australian treaty to New Zealand, and in my opinion that was not as satisfactory as a separate treaty. I am glad the minister is making a separate treaty, and I am also glad that he has made a new treaty with Australia. Everyone has now come to the conclusion that we cannot get out of the present depression by stifling international trade, and we in Canada have agreed that the first way to build up trade is to extend our trade within the empire. Now that everyone in Canada has accepted the policy; now that both sides of the house have agreed on the principle, I hope the minister will have absolutely no trouble. The people of British Columbia should be very well satisfied, though the Fraser valley milk producers may have some grievances; as their condensed milk production is now highly developed.
Butter is on an export basis to-day, due to the lack of prosperity in this dominion. I find from the statistics issued by this government that butter consumption has dropped from 350,000,000 pounds to 217,000,000 pounds, which is a tremendous drop in domestic consumption. Little wonder that we are on an export basis; little wonder that export prices prevail. May I point out to hon. members that when prosperity reigns in Canada our industrial workers undoubtedly consume a larger amount of our agricultural products. Under the conditions which existed from 1922 to 1929, there was an excellent market in Canada for all dairy products, and it was only because prices were high here that New Zealand was anxious to export butter to Canada rather than to England. Now, with the industrial depression which my hon. friend is trying to help relieve by the creation of a market in New Zealand for certain manufactured goods, we have at home an added market for agricultural products, but our surplus supplies must still compete in the markets of the world with the products of New Zealand, Denmark and every other dairying country.
That is the situation. The New Zealand treaty was cancelled by the late government for two reasons, first because it was due for readjustment and secondly because the terms of' the general treaty with Australia were no longer applicable to New Zealand. We had hoped to negotiate a new treaty in a very short time. I am not going to chide the
