minister for having let two years go by before bringing in this treaty. I know the difficulties with which he has been confronted, but now the question comes up as to whether under the new treaty or not he has lessened the sacrifice that was supposed to be made by the farmers of Canada under the old treaty. The farmers' wives in this dominion were told in the election that their pin money, their household money, came from butter, and that the iniquitous government which allowed this flood of New Zealand butter to come in was depriving them of a good deal of that money. My hon. friend has thrown his protective arm around the farmers' wife with a five cent tariff on butter. I compliment him on it, but I do not think it matters *whether the duty is five or ten cents, because we are now on an export basis and it will take a considerable period of prosperity before Canadians will consume all the butter that is made in this country and again be on an import basis. I had not the pleasure of being present when wool was being discussed, but the farmers themselves, were told that if we in this country would follow the protective tariff system and grade down our tariffs all the way from textiles to wool, there could be protection for the farmer; they were told that there would be benefits to the farmer through a tariff on wool. Whether or not my hon. friend is going to put a duty on wool when the Imperial conference comes on, I do not know. But I do know this, that the promise which was made by hon. gentlemen opposite that, if it was to apply to textiles, it should apply right down the scale to wool, has not been kept. After listening to the speech of my hon. friend from Dufferin, about how cheaply milk and wool were produced in New Zealand, I am afraid that if the minister has given some protection to the dairy farmer's wife on her butter he has left the farmer himself to face the full force of the New Zealand competition on wool. In other words, the producer of wool is granted nothing under this treaty. My hon. friend knows that the countries from which raw wool would come would be New Zealand and Australia, should we develop the spinning of wool extensively in Canada. Certain manufacturers in this dominion have constantly said that the whole Canadian clip, of which there is a tremendous surplus in storage at the present time, could be used in Canada. It is not being used however, and the fact remains that wool growers are still open to competition from New Zealand. Nevertheless I still believe the minister has worked out a fairly
good treaty. As a party we did not promise protection on wool, nor did we promise protection on butter, but we truthfully explained that there were certain benefits to be derived from trade treaties.
I do not know that the minister could have made a better treaty than he has. He had to sacrifice something; he could not have everything; and I was indeed delighted to hear him say in his opening remarks that, in order to make the treaty, there had to be a certain amount of give and take. I am going to compliment the minister on the treaty. I think his terms in connection with the automobile industry', with the lumber industry, and in connection with pulp and paper, some of which terms are the same as under the old treaty, are very good terms. I think that he has added to the list of goods for which we desire favourable entry into New Zealand, many commodities which were not included in the Australian treaty and for which the manufacturers had asked favourable consideration when the treaty was under revision. In fact, I believe the treaty is probably as good a treaty as could be made, and when it is considered item by item the minister will be able to explain the changes satisfactorily to the committee.
I do submit in conclusion, however, that no treaty, that we may make with any country is going to be as valuable a treaty, if the rates are uncertain, as if they were fixed. It is difficult for me to comment at the present time, not having studied the New Zealand terms and privileges under her customs laws, Knowing the embargoes that have been placed against imports by Australia and New Zealand, knowing the difficulties of these governments on occasion, and the means they have had to resort to-it is not easy for me, to have the faith in the productive results of this treaty, under these circumstances, that I should like. If there were an absolute assurance such as there should be if, for the short term of one year, that terms of the treaty would be carried out without restrictions of any kind; that the right was denied to either country to put in any new tariffs restrictions or embargoes, I should like the treaty better. I do submit to the minister that, with his keen desire to see this trade a success. With the reasonably favourable terms which he has made and on which he has a right to be complimented by the people of the dominion, he should not allow orders in council, or the privileges and powers under the extraordinary legislation which exists at the present time,

to hamper the business of Canada by applying the dumping or valuation clause. Let business flow, under the terms of the agreement and I think the treaty will be a success.

I think it is clear from this article that it is this writer's opinion that the advantages, so far as New Zealand is concerned, are for New Zealand farmers, and so far as Canada is concerned, for the manufacturers of Canada. In other words, the concessions given

by Canada are at the expense of the farmers of Canada, if tariffs on the farm products are of any assistance, as members of the party opposite have always claimed so persistently. As I read the terms of the treaty now before us, wool is placed on the free list while blankets bear a rate of 22j per cent; wool travelling rugs, 30 per cent and wool floor and carpet rugs, 25 per cent. In view of the discussion which took place in this house on February 22, I am unable to understand why this treaty should contain these provisions. On that date the following resolution was moved by the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Swanston):
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government of the Dominion of Canada place a duty on raw wool that would reasonably protect the Canadian wool growers.
That resolution was adopted by a vote of the house. In speaking thereon, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) said:
Is it worth while to do something to keep alive this industry into which these men have put so much?
The hon. minister was referring to the sheep growers.
Personally, I feel that it is. If they were not efficient it would be a different thing, but they are as efficient as the sheep farmers of any country in the world. I have no hesitation in stating that we should put forward every effort to keep this industry alive.

I feel that any tariff that will protect the wool industry must be on the whole schedule of wool from wool in the grease, w-ool scoured, wool tops, yarns and so forth. I therefore appreciate this opportunity to put myself on record as being in favour of the resolution.

Wool from New Zealand has been coming in free of duty and it will continue to come in free of duty. The question I have in mind has direct application to the present discussion. [Mi Stevens.]
As I understand it, the currency of New Zealand at the moment is at a lower point than that of Great Britain, and the difficulty in connection with the exchange that existed with regard to Great Britain would exist, I imagine, to a greater degree with regard to New Zealand. Did any discussion take ijdace on that point, or was there any suggestion that it might be necessary to take action with respect to New Zealand as was the case with respect to Great Britain?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I think I can explain that in a few sentences. The exchange situation in New Zealand has obtained for some considerable time, much longer than it has in England. I think it is acknowledged by all students of the subject that following a depreciation of currency prices will adjust themselves and price levels will rise.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: In the country where the depreciated currency exists.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Yes, where the depreciation occurs. There is usually a considerable lag between the time they go off the gold standard, say, or whatever causes the depreciation, and the time when the price levels will have adjusted themselves to the new standard. In New Zealand that situation largely obtains; the price levels have risen not altogether but in substantial measure to a degree commensurate with the depreciation of the currency.
My hon. friend from Macleod this afternoon referred to the time when England went off the gold standard. If I may use the expression, England went off the gold standard with a bang. There was no notice given; she just went off that standard between Saturday night and Monday morning, and the currency depreciated very rapidlju It went down with one plunge to a very low point; there was not a gradual decline such as occurred in New Zealand, for instance; the decline was very sudden. Between the time of that sudden sharp decline and the time that prices, through purchases of raw material and so forth abroad, could begin to adjust themselves, there was an opportunity for profiteers, if you like, to take undue advantage of that situation in dealing with British goods, to their own individual advantage and to the injury of the country to which the goods were sent. This dominion recognized that fact, as did other countries, and we stabilized the pound for the time being at $4.86, or par value. Some little time having elapsed, we later allowed the price for exchange values to be $4.40.
I do not desire to argue to-night whether or not that was the correct thing to do, or whether it was right or wrong, but I do want

to point out the difference in the two cases. maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Just one question; I do not want to delay the committee. May I ask if the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe and the hon. member for Haldimand approve of this treaty?

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: They are two very fine members, but may I tell the minister that during the session of 1930 those two hon. members were sent to Manitoba, to Quebec, to Nova Scotia and practically all over the country by the Conservative organization directed by General McRae, who is now in the other house, to tell the farmers of Canada as a whole that if the Conservative party came into power, New Zealand and Australian butter would not come into this country. I do not take the minister very seriously when he says the depreciated currency of New Zealand will have no effect. We have an example in what has been done in England, and that twenty per cent advantage in exchange will bring down the duty on butter. I think before this treaty is finally passed those two hon. members who spoke on this subject so often during the campaign should state their views regarding this treaty. An immense amount of literature was sent out from this building with regard to the importation of New Zealand butter, and I think the whole matter should be looked into in order to see whether those two hon. gentlemen were trying to get into power or whether they were really in earnest in the remarks they made.

speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I had in mind also the statement made last year by the minister in reference to Australia, whose currency was depreciated. Australia was stated by the minister to have a very material advantage over Canada in the oriental market because of the position of her currency. So, like the hon. member who has just spoken, while I hope the situation will not be complicated by the exchange I am not quite certain in spite of the explanation just given.
While I am on my feet I want to say one word about one phase of the treaty itself. It is unfortunate, but I think it is unavoidable, that in making such trade treaties with our sister dominions of New Zealand and Australia, we are inevitably confronted with this difficulty: in the main, the goods which they must sell-leaving out a long list of smaller items-the goods to which they must attach overwhelming importance must be such commodities as meats, dairy products, wool, hides and other products of the farm; and if they are to get any advantage at all from the treaty they must increase the sales of these articles in this country. This is an important matter, and I appreciate that it is unavoidable when you are dealing with these two countries whose exports are of that kind.
I understand, of course, that industrial conditions in this country will be improved by the treaty and the farmers will, of course, receive some indirect benefit. There will be an increase in employment and greater purchasing power among those engaged in industry in Canada, and that will, in a degree, make up for any loss the farmers may suffer. But at the same time I cannot close my eyes to the fact that it is impossible to make a treaty with these countries without, so far as expense is concerned, making it at the direct expense of agriculture and for the direct benefit of other vocations. The amount of indirect benefit the farmers will receive is unknown, and undoubtedly it will be a counterbalancing factor, but I do hope that the minister, in the interests of Canada, and of agriculture particularly, will keep a very close eye on the importations of dairy and other products such as wool, which will come into the country. Wool will oome in free while under the same treaty woollen blankets made from that wool will enter under a considerably protected tariff. I hope the minister will see to it that if it does reach the point where agriculture is threatened without some compensating advantage, some other arrangements will be made; because we all hope that, while the manufacturers of our country will receive the full advantage of the treaty and will prosper, they will not obtain that prosperity over a tariff wall to the disadvantage of the farmers. I trust that this *will be kept in mind when the treaty is in operation.

In a treaty of this kind, I do not know that I would have very much complaint about making certain sacrifices for the fishing industry, the lumber industry and some others that we have in Canada. But what about the automobile industry? We have a tariff on automobiles, and the manufacturers take full advantage of it when they sell cars to farmers and others in Canada. It is very easy to demonstrate that they do take full advantage of the tariff, and on the other hand we are sacrificing to some extent to give them markets abroad. There is an Imperial conference coming and it is just possible that there will be a chance to even things up by means of some arrangement between Canada and other parts of the empire, possibly Great Britain, and I trust that some of these manufacturers at least will be willing to give way in some cases, if it is necessary, in order to assist agriculture.

maintopic: NEW ZEALAND TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I want to add my protest to the protest made this afternoon against the principle of this section. This section would not be so bad if the provisions of section 6 of the Customs Tariff Act of Canada had not been completely changed and distorted out of their original application by a change in the sections from 36 to 43, which provide now that the price to be fixed for duty purposes shall be, not simply the domestic price, the usual price in the country -of origin, but any arbitrary price that may be

fixed by the minister. Under these circumstances, this treaty is going to be subject to all the fluctuations and instability of other items in the tariff schedule of this country', and it is a poor beginning in making a treaty, particularly one which at most is to run but for one year, to inject into it such an element of uncertainty as is contained in the provision that section 6 of the Customs Tariff Act may apply. Section 6 permits not only the charging of the difference between the invoice price of the article and the proper domestic price of the article as sold in the country of origin, but the charging of the difference between the invoice price and any arbitrary price which may be fixed by the minister. That is a poor principle to introduce into a treaty, especially a treaty of such short duration as this; and in the interests of stability and of good relations between the countries concerned it would be most desirable to leave this out. Stabilization of tariffs was one of the things on which our friends opposite went into power, but stabilization of tariffs and of economic conditions has been about the last thing they have accomplished, and I do not think that our sister dominion of New Zealand should have such a condition imposed upon her. My hon. friend says that New Zealand has consented to it, but I say that we should not place Canada in the position of having to exercise such a power as is given here. Let me give an example. Suppose any shipment of goods-I will not specify any commodity' -comes from New Zealand, bought by a consumer in this country at an invoice price which he believes is right, and for some reason or other a manufacturer or producer in Canada makes representation to the government, while the goods are on the water, with the result that notice is given under this section. When* the importer comes to pay duty on those goods which he has purchased at a certain price and has probably resold, he finds that section 6 of the Customs Act has been applied, the dumping duty has been put on, and he is subject to loss under the contract of resale which he has made. I submit that that is not good for the consumer in this country, neither is it good for the relations with other dominions. I protest against the principle contained in this article, which makes it not only elastic but introduces into our trade treaties the jumping-jack provision, if I may so term it, contained in section 6 of the Customs Act.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: There is a specific duty of five cents a pound. The differentiation in exchange would perhaps account for something in the neighbourhood of three cents or a little better, provided-and this is where, 1 think, some hon. members in discussing the question have overlooked an important factor -provided there had been no changes in the price levels in the country where the depreciated currency obtains. I am quite certain the price levels in New Zealand have risen considerably. That is an indefinite and more or less indefinable factor, but it has seriously affected the advantage gained by the depreciated currency. It would be very difficult to give a precise answer, but I think one may say the actual protection is in the neighbourhood of four cents.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND

speechtext: I do not know whether I am correctly informed or not, but I understand the New Zealand currency is 20 per cent depreciated with respect to our currency. maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND

I referred to binder twine and stated that there was an apparent drawback to the use of this hemp in that it tended to ruffle or ball up when passing through the eye of the binder.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: What is the present duty on hemp?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: It is free.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: If it is free to all countries, why does it appear here?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Stability.

Item agreed to.
Schedule A-Customs tariff, Canada-ex. 549. Wool, not further prepared than combed: free.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: How much wool comes in from New Zealand under this item?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I have only the percentages. In 1931, about one-hailf of the total imports of 2,856,000 pounds of wool in the grease came in from New Zealand; of a total importation of 5,590,000 pounds of washed wool, about 9 per cent came from New Zealand.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Has the minister the percentages for Australia?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
The imports during 193031 of wool in the grease from Australia amounted to 496,000 pounds. I might state that a large amount of the wool from New Zealand and Australia finds access to our markets through the United States or London.
. Mr. SPENCER: What is the tariff on wool coming from New Zealand?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: There is no tariff.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
Again I wonder at what has become of the hon. gentlemen who about a week or so ago voted for a tariff on wool.
Mr. VENIOT; They kept away to-night.
[Mr. Young. 1

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: There are quite a few of them here, but we have not heard a single protest.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: They are all subdued.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: We on this side of the chamber are not afraid of free wool or anything else, but I am surprised at hon. gentlemen going to all the trouble they did to have a duty imposed, and then remaining silent when an item like this comes before the committee.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: What is the good of putting a duty on wool and then taking it off? Putting a duty on will cause the shippers to ship direct, and that is all the difference it will make.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: We have not taken any duty off wool; it was free across the board. We are proposing, and we hope it will be carried in a day or two, an intermediate tariff of ten cents a pound and a general tariff of fifteen cents a pound, and we hope that these rates will divert the business direct to this country. We do not desire to interfere with or touch the British preferential tariff until after the Imperial economic conference.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Practically all our work of a week or so ago in getting a duty put on wool has turned out to be eyewash-it does not amount to anything at all because tonight we are taking the duty off. We are simply saying: You cannot come in through the back door, you must come in through the front.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
It seems to me that this action demonstrates to the country just how serious members were when they voted for the resolution, which was carried by a large majority. As a matter of fact, I do not think the government ever has cared very much about the wool grower. It will be remembered that a short time ago the government introduced a system of fixing an arbitrary rate of exchange in connection with the valuing of imports for duty purposes, and they passed an order in council which fixed the value of the pound at $4.40. The manufacturers of worsted and other goods made representations to the government and asked that while this valuation should apply to the finished article which they were manufacturing, it should not apply to the raw material. In other words, the Canadian wool grower was not to have the same protection given to the manufacturer. As an indication of how solicitous this government is of the wool growers, they

New Zealand Trade Agreement
passed an order in council on January 8, the last clause of which reads:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the order in council, and as an exemption thereto, the value of the pound sterling for the purposes of application of special duty on all shipments from Great Britain to Canada of wool, not further prepared than combed, shall be the average value thereof.
And yet the government has stipulated that in connection with other commodities the value of the pound shall be fixed at $4.40 I think we have the right to inquire from those hon. gentlemen who were so vociferous for a duty on wool why they are not protesting to-night against this item. Perhaps they want to let the minister get through his treaty; periiaps the discipline is such that they do not want to interfere. I think it would be more in the interests of the wool growers if they voiced their opinions when these ' schedules are before the committee rather than on an abstract resolution.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
Would it be correct to say
that practically 30 per cent of our imports of wool come from New Zealand?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I do not think so.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
I think that statement was
made in a recent debate.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: The percentage of washed wool is 9, and the percentage of wool in the grease a little over half; it would not average 30 per cent, as the total imports of wool in the grease were 2,800,000 pounds, and washed or scoured wool, 5,590,000 pounds.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
Has the minister any
information as to how much wool from New Zealand comes in through the United States?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
I have had some of my
staff working for months on that and other similar problems. It is very difficult to ascertain, but we have figures indicating quite a substantial quantity. Wool being on the free list, it is impossible to follow it.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
What quantity comes
from the United States?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I have not the percentage of wool in the grease from the United States, but 20 per cent of washed wool comes from there. The quantity of wool in the grease coming from the United States is 511,000 pounds.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
When this
bill was first introduced I felt like congratulating the government on their apparent change of heart in at last deciding that we must trade with some other country, but I could
not help noticing, as we went through the items, the minister remarking in the great majority of cases, "no importations." I wonder if, after all, anyone in Canada will benefit from this treaty. If so, who?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: As I think I stated before, when I say "no importations," that means no goods coming into Canada. The story as regards exports is different. The largest value of the treaty will be under the British preference, general articles not included in this schedule, a very wide range.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
The minister must
realize that the sheep men will be somewhat disappointed at this item in the treaty. I am sure he understands the situation, and I hope when this item is under discussion at the imperial conference, some assistance will be given to the sheep men. Our sheep raisers are operating at present at a tremendous loss, and my information is that most of them will be out of business shortly unless they get some help in this respect.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
I notice in 1930 we imported from New Zealand, in round figures,
1,900,000	pounds, and in 1931, 1,744,000 pounds. Roughly speaking, that is the wool off the backs of about 200,000 sheep, and this is quite an item. I think the minister should have it in mind when he is considering the welfare of the sheep industry.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
Wool, I take it, is like
some other commodities that have a habit of finding their way from all over the world to large central markets. Buyers go to those markets and select the kinds of wool they want. According to this year's budget, it is the intention to impose a duty of fifteen cents a pound on wool under the general tariff. New Zealand wool to a large extent comes in through the United States; that is, it finds its way to the United States market where the buyers go and select what they want. Under this arrangement and the clause in the treaty which we discussed earlier in the evening, requiring direct shipment to Canada, it will be impossible for the buyers for our wool manufacturers to get the wool in the most convenient market, and it might be very awkward for them to have to go to New Zealand and select it there. In that regard there is a danger of doing real injury to our wool industry.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
I should like to ask to
what extent this wool coming from New Zealand competes with the average wool grown in Canada?
New Zealand Trade Agreement

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: There is no doubt it does compete, but the whole subject of wool is very complex. I have been amazed in studying the question to find the varieties of wool it is necessary to have to produce even a given article. Carpets, which are looked upon as comparatively simple, require wool to be imported from, I think, India, to give them a certain lustre, pile and so forth. Therefore in manufacturing you must have a variety of wool. While there is undoubtedly some competition between New Zealand and Canadian wools, there is still a marked difference between the wools. It would be impossible for me, without careful preparation, to give an exact description of it, but I can assure my hon. friend there is a great difference in the types of wool produced.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Where wool is not competing, it should be brought info Canada free for manufacturing purposes, but the minister knows wool is being sold in Canada below cost-

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I realize item 538 has been passed, but I did not at the time know that it had been called' passed by the Chair. Would the minister mind telling me, if it is not too much trouble, how much binder twine, if any, has been imported from New Zealand in the last few years? I was not aware that we were importing any.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: None from New Zealand.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Is there any prospect of manufactured binder twine coming from there?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I think the main export will be the raw sisal or hemp.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I notice the rate under the general tariff is to be fifteen cents. This is a change which the minister intends to make at some future date in the duty on wool.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: It will be passed when the budget schedules are under consideration.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: It seems strange to me, when the farmer in the west is getting about four cents a pound on his wool that a duty of fifteen -cents a pound should be imposed' on that commodity. But when you are getting no wool from foreign countries except what comes in indirectly from New Zealand or Australia through the United States, and when it practically all comes in under -the British preference, this is ia camouflage -to make the farmers think -they are getting some concession.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
Just to show the small quantity of wool of similar quality that enters

Canada in competition with our own wool, I have under my hand the figures for 1927, which I think are the latest:
Leicester, Cotswold, Lincolnshire, South Down combing wools, or wools known as lustre wools, and other like combing wools, such as are grown in Canada:
Quantity imported	Value
259 pounds	$93
If hon. gentlemen who contend for duties on wool would pay some attention to that fact, it might modify -their opinion.

Item agreed to.
Schedule A-Customs tariff, Canada-553. Blankets of any material, not to include 'automobile rugs, steamer rugs nor similar articles: 22J per cent.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
It will be noticed that the -previous items are free, but when we come to manufactured articles they have to carry duties of 22^,	30 and 25 per
cent. Could >the minister not have made a better deal than this, particularly when our Canadian manufacturers enjoy free raw material? I am not asking for 'any protection for the farmer or for anybody else, but I want to protest against this discrimination. The moment we -come to a fully manufactured article, up goes the duty. The manufacturer must always have a tremendous amount of protection or we are -told he cannot live, I have a list of the items of farm produce all of which come in free, but the very -moment we strike wool or wool blankets or wool fabrics wholly manufactured the duty is -put up over twenty per cent. I certainly protest against that. While I am in agreement with the arrangement which the minister has made, I do think this is giving entirely too much protection to men who enjoy the -privilege of getting in their raw material without paying one -cent of duty.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: How much came in under this item from New Zealand last year, and what duty do they charge against our blankets?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
- What is the duty the other way?

New Zealand Trade Agreement

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: It is rather difficult to get (he exact classification, but I -presume that this one would cover it; "rugs, n.e.i., not supplied for floor covering." We get a rate of twenty per cent ad valorem.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
There is just one point I should like to mention in reference to the question which has been raised as to the different treatment accorded under our tariffs to raw wool, for instance, and the manufactured article. I am not going to go into that whole question except to say that naturally enough, it has aroused a good deal of interest and discussion, and a good many suggestions have been made as to how, seeing that we are on a protective tariff and must be in view of conditions throughout the world to-day, the benefit may be passed along right down the line to those who carry on what is certainly an industry indigenous to this country, that is the growing of the wool itself.
I would like to make a suggestion which I have made more than once, and which I believe has merit. It is that when protection is afforded to a manufacturer, such as the manufacturer of woollen goods or of any other article the raw material of which is found in whole or in part in this country, the protection be granted upon a sliding scale and vary in accordance with the percentage of the native raw material used in the production of the manufactured article. I do believe, Mr. Chairman, that if an arrangement of that kind were made, after careful study, of course it would pass down the line to the original producer himself some of the advantages of our present fiscal system, of which the .original producer at the present time has all too few. It would also encourage the greater use of our own raw materials and would inflict little hardship on the manufacturers themselves. If Iby so arranging the tariff that the position of the manufacturer was more advantageous the greater the percentage of Canadian raw materials he used, in manufactures, of course, where Canadian raw material could be used, such as wool, and less advantageous the greater the percentage he used of raw material brought in from outside, I believe one of the greatest objections of the farmers to the protective tariff would be largely removed. I believe also that it would encourage such native industries as the growing of wool, as well as increase the market for raw hides and leather goods and other articles manufactured in this -country. This question is worthy of consideration, and if it could be worked out I believe it would redound to the great advantage of this country.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Those members of the house who think they are serving the interests of the farmer by asking for more protection on the things he has to sell are making a grave mistake. They know or ought to know that the price of farm products cannot be enhanced by high tariffs. They have preached that themselves many times, and to say that the farmer will consent to higher protection on manufactured goods in order to obtain a worthless protection on his own products is utter nonsense.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman did not catch my meaning. I was suggesting lower protection when the manufacturer did not use Canadian raw material.

Item agreed to.
Schedule A-Customs tariff, Canada-ex. 572. Rugs, floor or carpet, of wool: 25 per cent.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Are Sarouk rugs included under this item?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I do not think so.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: Because the clerk of the house bought a rug for $480. I do not know whether it came from Australia, but it was a pretty expensive rug.
Item agreed to.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA

speechtext:
Schedule B-Customs tariff, New Zealand-[DOT] 35. Fish, viz:-
(3)	Fish, potted, and preserved viz., salmon, iiieluding any liquor, oil, or sauce, lfd. per pound.
(4)	Fish, potted, and preserved, n.e.i., including any liquor, oil, or sauce, 2d. per pound.
(Note-The term "fish" is used in the tariff in its widest sense, and includes shell-fish, crustaceans, and other foods obtained from the fisheries.)

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am beginning to regret, I am sorry to say, the eulogies I passed on the minister this afternoon; for I am afraid now that we in British Columbia are going to come at the wrong end of this agreement. The preference given to our canned salmon is very small. We allow the New Zealand toheroa,. which is entirely a luxury, to come in absolutely free. It competes, I am told, with the higher class of lobsters, and people who can afford to have lobster suppers these hard times can afford to pay a duty. But we are allowing toheroas to come in free, and New Zealand gives us only a very small preference on our salmon. It amounts to only one penny and a quarter per pound. There is a higher duty on item 35 (4). That would apply to tinned herrings and tinned pilchards, for which we are anxious on the Pacific coast

New Zealand, Trade Agreement
to get a market. Pilchards and herring are naturally low priced fish and the duty of twopence a pound would be quite considerable. We get a preference of only a penny a pound there, which is not very material. In the Australian treaty, as the minister is aware, he secured for us a preference of three pence a pound, or 6 cents, on salmon, which was really substantial, and, I believe, has enabled British Columbia to secure the greater part of the market.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: It will be remembered when the Australian treaty was up I took exception jO what I thought then was sectional legislation-favouring the Pacific coast in the matter of salmon more than it did the east coast in the matter of crustaceans. The minister told me that it was too late, that the treaty had been signed and he could not take the matter up, but he would endeavour later on to see if Australia would come to any different agreement. Did he consider that last year when he discussed this matter with New Zealand, and am I mistaken in thinking that crustaceans put up in cans have not the same preference as salmon put up in cans?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
There is a very slight
variation, my hon. friend will notice. I can assure him that the whole question was threshed out at great length during the discussion of this agreement. The position of New Zealand is that canned salmon is an essential food commonly used, and not competitive with any New Zealand fish.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Are crustaceans?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes, in a sense they are.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Where do they get them?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
They therefore give a
quarter of a penny lower rate on salmon than on the other fish.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Do sardines get the same
rate as salmon?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I think item 35 (4) would
include sardines.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Twopence a pound?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Where is the competition
with anything in New Zealand in 'the matter of sardines? They do not put up sardines, and they have been importing very large quantities from Canada in past years. With the New Brunswick sardine we took the Australian market from the Netherlands. Now this is going to put us out of that market.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Oh, no.
[Mr Neill.)

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: I cannot see that.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: It will allow the Netherlands to compete very strongly against us. In the face of that, notwithstanding the difference here in this preference between sardines and salmon, you have the extra cost imposed under the budget on the containers, which for sardines are more costly than for salmon.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: My hon. friend will notice that that does not apply on goods going out, only on goods coming into Canada.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: But you have to apply for a drawback of 99 per cent. Why put them to that trouble?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
New Zealand does not
follow that practice I am told.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: What practice?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
The practice my hon.
friend is mentioning. Australia does, but not New Zealand.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: What practice?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: With regard to containers.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: We impose it on our people.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: That is an additional protection here.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I fail to see it. I enter
my strong protest against what appears to be sectional legislation. What is good for the Pacific coast ought to be good for the eastern coast of Canada, and the minister has no right to enter into an agreement by which a difference is made between sea food on the western coast and sea food on the eastern coast of Canada. Our fishing industry on the eastern coast along the Atlantic is in such a depressed condition to-day that the fishermen need all the encouragement possible, and even a quarter of a penny would help them.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: We have not changed the rates at all from what they were before we went on the general tariff; we have restored the old rates instead of the general tariff.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
If it was wrong then, why
should it continue now?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I agree with my hon.
friend.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I protest on behalf of the
fishermen of the maritime provinces, especially in regard to the sardine and lobster fisheries. It is an outrage.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Are these various rates
under (3) and (4), item 35, specific?

New Zealand Trade Agreement

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: They are British preferential rates.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
We cannot alter their
ideas of the British preference.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: No.

Item agreed to.
Schedule B-Customs tariff, New Zealand- 35 (4). Fish, potted, and preserved, n.e.i., including any liquor, oil, or sauce, 2d. per pound.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I want to add a word
on this item to what I said on No. 123. Item 123 it will be remembered covers canned whitebait and canned crayfish at 15 per cent ad valorem but with a limit of not more than 7J cents per pound. I pointed out that this is 2i per cent below the British preference on these goods coming into Canada. When we sell our canned fish under 35 (4) to New Zealand we have a straight specific duty of twopence per pound, whether the fish is cheap or dear, plus 22i per cent surtax. I submit that that is not fair to those who are producing canned fish in this country. It must be remembered that we are more and more developing the packing of fish in cans, even the cheaper qualities, and a specific duty is particularly hard on this fish.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Herring especially.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: And pilchards.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, and other fish as
well. The minister says we are only restoring the old duty, but the point is these articles were not subject to any previous arrangement, as I understand it. He is now making a treaty with New Zealand for the first time with regard to these commodities, and therefore is in a position to ask New Zealand to give us a quid pro quo. But it does seem to me as if the most of the giving is done by ourselves.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: No.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: I am speaking of the fish items. We are reducing the duty below the British preferential rate on their fish, but on our fish they are keeping their duty up under the British preference and that British preference is much higher against us than our British preference is against them. Therefore I submit, first, even if our duty were not below the British preference it still would be lower than the duty the New Zealander imposes against Canadian fish, and secondly, we are giving them a duty below the British preference. I protest against it because I submit there is quite a business to be developed, particularly on the part of the maritime province fishermen in connection with lobsters and other fish-sardines my hon. friend has already mentioned.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: And large herring.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Even the albaeore or tuna is now being canned. It seems to me we might develop quite a market in New Zealand for various sorts of canned fish.

Item agreed to.
Schedule B-Customs tariff, New Zealand- 137. Hosiery, viz: socks or stockings of silk or artificial silk: 32i per cent ad valorem.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: I notice the New Zealand duty under the general rate is 67.3 per cent, while under the treaty we will be able to export our goods at 39.8 per cent, leaving a net advantage to our manufacturers of about 27| per cent. Has the minister any assurance from our manufacturers that they can compete in New Zealand on that basis?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: It is expected that they can.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Have they given any
assurance to that effect?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes. We rather excel in the manufacture of hosiery.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Then we do not need quite such a heavy protective duty ourselves.

Item agreed to.
Schedule B-Customs tariff, New Zealand- 196. Boots, shoes, clogs, pattens, slippers, shoettes, sandals, galoshes, overshoes, and other footwear, n.e.i.: 25 per cent ad valorem.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: I want to ask the same question in this regard. The New Zealand general tariff is 61.3 per cent; our goods will enter at 30.6 per cent, leaving almost a 31 per cent advantage. Have our manufacturers given any assurance that they can compete on that basis?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: We will remember this when the time comes to consider our -own tariff.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: The items are passed, but I should like to know why we are allowing raw furs to be brought into Canada free while if we widh to ship furs to New Zealand we have a pretty stiff duty against us; in fact it is almost prohibitive.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I hesitate very much to criticise any duty that New Zealand chooses to enforce; my hon. friend will appreciate that. There is no doubt that the general level of their duties is pretty high, but the tariff
New Zealand Trade Agreement

is their chief source of revenue, and for that reason they insist on maintaining these duties. It will be noticed that in many instances the major portion of the duty is made Up of additional surtaxes, which have been put on for emergency purposes.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I quite
appreciate that New Zealand is not engaged in manufacturing to a great extent, but throughout this whole treaty raw products entering New Zealand carry a duty, while in our case we let practically all their raw products enter Canada free. I do not object to that because 1 do not believe we should put a duty on raw products at all, and as a matter of fact I do not think we should have a very heavy duty on anything. It does seem to me, however, that we are not getting a very great advantage by including some of these articles. Certainly there will be no advantage to the raw fur dealer in Canada.

Item agreed to.
Schedule B-Customs tariff. New Zealand- 292. Paper-pulp, for the manufacture of paper: free.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: In British Columbia we would have been very glad if we could have obtained some concession in connection with this item. It appears here on the free list, but there is nothing in that because it is free from all over the world, so we get no preference. New Zealand has a tariff item, No. 284, which reads, "paper, namely bleached sulphite or similar paper which is to be used in the manufacture of twine or imitation wickerware." That enters New Zealand free, but only if it is to be used for those purposes. I do not quite see how it could be described as "similar paper" if it is to be used in the manufacture of those articles, but we would have been very glad to obtain a concession in that regard. We call that material pulp or sulphite. Was the question discussed as to whether or not we could export bleached sulphite under this item, if it was not to be used for the manufacture of twine or imitation wickerware?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: I cannot say very much about that, but I may tell my hon. friend that the paper schedule is very satisfactory to the people here in Canada.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: In the west?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: To those who do not make paper, but who only make sulphite pulp?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes. There is some question regarding pulp, but I do not think it would be fair to New Zealand to disclose all that was privately discussed between the minister and myself. This was the best that could be done under the circumstances.

Item agreed to.

(1)	Cultivators; harrows; ploughs; drills;

The surtax to be levied, collected and paid under section five of the Customs Acts Amendment Act, 1930, on the goods included in tariff item numbered 333	(1) shall be an amount equal to onetwentieth of the total duty of customs otherwise chargeable.

mouldboard plates unbent, steel share-plates cut to pattern, skeith-plates, plough beam forgings, and discs for harrows or ploughs, free.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Again the same question, Mr. Chairman: The New Zealand tariff is 42.87 per cent, while the treaty rate will be 36.75 per cent, leaving an advantage of 6.12 per cent to our Canadian manufacturers. I suppose they can compete on that basis?

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: We would have liked a much better rate but that was the best we could get. There are two plants of considerable size in New Zealand manufacturing these articles, and the New Zealand government desired to maintain a fairly good protection for them.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: The British preference is only 10 per cent.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: But Great Britain does not compete very seriously in that class of goods.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: As a matter of fact this is an arrangement as good as we have had in the past, and our manufacturers have sent veiy considerable quantities of farm implements to that country.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes, but more under the next item.

Item agreed to.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I would like to
ask the minister if this item includes poles and pilings. A good deal of lumber of that kind is shipped to the United States.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: I am under the impression that poles, piling and that sort of timber would come under the general British preference.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Of course the minister is
aware of the fact that the success of this item depends upon the continuation of the subsidies to the steamships running to Australia and New Zealand. There was no item for this amount in the main estimates, and I think it behooves the government to place an item in the supplementaries.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Last month we did one
hundred per cent of Australia's soft timber business, and the month before we did ninety-eight per cent. We are really controlling that business very satisfactorily and this item will make it easier to do business with New Zealand. We have not paid any subsidies on Australian steamship lines in the past year.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the
government not to pay subsidies this year? I have here very strong resolutions passed by the lumber people of British Columbia which do not sustain the attitude of the minister.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Those have more to do
with the China service, but in any case the matter is under consideration for the supplementaries.
Item agreed to.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I just want to sum up
in a word, so that the committee may understand at least as I view it, what is the net result of these changes. I do not retract anything that has been said; I fully concur in the Statement that an agreement is at all times desirable. If this means good will, better feeling and a likelihood of more trade with New Zealand, then by all means let us have it; but I do not think we ought to fool ourselves as to the net result of all these items in the schedules which have been passed.
I have gone over the items quickly and I think the net result of these schedules, both A and B, is this. First, with regard to goods coming into Canada, the result is that on no fewer than twenty-six items the duty has been reduced-reduced on goods coming into this country in competition with Canadian goods. The duty has been reduced even below the British preference rate and also below the old treaty rate, in so far as these items were contained in that treaty. The committee will bear that in mind. Twenty-six items in this schedule have been reduced for the benefit of New Zealand, so that .they are now below the regular British preference rate; and in the case of all items which were subject to the old treaty, they are reduced below the old treaty rate. Only two items have been increased, namely, the item for fresh meat and the item for butter; but even at that, both these items are still below the British preference rate. In regard to the fresn meat item, the British preference rate was
4	cents, and that has been reduced to 3 cents under the treaty. The old treaty rate was one-half cent. Butter is 8 cents under the British preference rate and that has been reduced to 5 cents. The old treaty rate was one cent. Apricots and peaches, which were not mentioned as we were going through the items, are 2 cents under the British preference and 1 cent under the treaty. So that the net result is that 26 items have been reduced for the benefit of New Zealand, below the British preference, while two items have been increased over the old treaty rate but are still below the British preference. That is what we have done for New Zealand; those are the concessions we have made.
With regard to the item of butter, I would point out that the change to the 5 cent rate will be no protection whatever for this commodity unless we use the power provided for in article IV and fix an arbitrary value for duty purposes. With exchange as it is, the
5	cents will be practically wiped out. If that provision is used and that protection of 5 cents is maintained, then what I am afraid will happen is exactly what happened before, when the 8 cent rate was put on. The butter producer in this country was fooled into thinking that butter was the best thing to produce, and the result was that too much was produced for home consumption, with the inevitable consequence that we went on the export market, and down went the price. That will probably happen under this 5 cent tariff rate. No one knows better than the butter producers of this country, after the last two years' experience, just what will
New Zealand Trade Agreement

happen. The duty of 8 cents did not bring them the prosperity they expected but just the reverse. In fact it was more duty than they asked for, as was pointed out this afternoon in an extract read by an hon. member. Let me read a statement made by Mr. Robinson, the president of the National Dairy Council, at a meeting in Winnipeg. He said:
It has been our opinion that three or four years must elapse before we could make up the deficiency of nearly 50,000,000 pounds of butter. The extra stimulus of the eight cent tariff, together with the enormous fall in grain prices, has caused, however, such a rapid increase in the butter made all over Canada that it now appears that we may be self-sustaining this season, and even have a surplus for export. This seems to be inevitable by next year at the latest. In all our arguments during the past few years, we have stated plainly that the effect of the tariff would be lost when export began. That is, in fact, the chief reason why we believed a four cent tariff to he more lasting than an eight cent one. We are now face to face with this condition.
At the moment, the export surplus of butter if of little value to Canadian farmers. It will cost them money this year. Thus, the immediate benefit to them of the tinkering with the New Zealand treaty that has so offended one of the best customers for our manufactured products is nil.
It is obvious that if Canada is to gain any net benefit from this rapid increase in butter production our dairymen must so improve their methods that they can meet the world on the basis of quality and price. It is conceded that this is possible but that the attainment of the ideal will be a matter of hard work over a term of years.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: It is a wonder he did not see that when he was protesting so strongly before.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
That was the statement made by Mr. Robinson, president of the National Dairy Council. And that was the result of the 8 cent duty. But there was one more result. During the last election campaign, and during the debate held in this house in 1930, tears were wept about the number of cows which had disappeared from Canada and had gone over the line. It was said that there had been a decrease in the cow population of the country of 102,000, and our friends on the other side never ceased to lament about it. Even the present Prime Minister was like little Bo Peep who had lost her sheep-he didn't know where these 100,000 cows had gone. Well, I have here a statement of the cow population of Canada for 1930 and 1931; and whereas there were 102,000 cows less in 192728, I find that the number of milch cows in Canada in 1930 was 3,683,000 as compared with 3,513,000 in 1931, when the 8 cent tariff was on. In other words, there was a loss of
170.000	cows in one year.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: We shall have to have an inquiry.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext: That was under the 8 cent tariff put on by this government. Coming back, therefore, to the outstanding features of this schedule, I say that the butter item is not by any means a sure Shot either for the benefit of the farmer or for the benefit of the consumer. It will be no protection if section 6 is not used, in view of the exchange, and it is a question whether it will do the farmer any good even if 'the 5 cent item is actually effective.

maintopic: TARIFF RATES ON GOODS THE PRODUCE OR MANUFACTURE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Is section 6 the dumping
clause?
